title: The Nurse Who Poisoned Leaded Gasoline's Lie
event_summary: At Standard Oil's Bayway refinery in Elizabeth, New Jersey, workers producing tetraethyl lead gasoline additive began hallucinating, convulsing, and dying — five killed and thirty-five hospitalized in a single week of October 1924. Industrial hygienist Alice Hamilton, who had spent decades documenting lead poisoning in factories, publicly confronted the chemical industry and testified that leaded gasoline posed a catastrophic public health threat to every person who breathed urban air. Despite her warnings and the gruesome deaths at Bayway, a compliant Surgeon General's panel declared leaded gasoline safe enough for sale after an industry-funded study lasting barely seven months.
why_forgotten: General Motors, Standard Oil, and DuPont — who jointly owned the Ethyl Corporation — waged an aggressive campaign to frame Hamilton as an alarmist and bury the Bayway deaths as an isolated industrial accident rather than a preview of mass environmental poisoning. For decades, industry-funded researchers dominated the conversation, and Hamilton's role was overshadowed by the later work of Clair Patterson in the 1960s. The episode was treated as a minor labor incident rather than the pivotal moment when corporations knowingly chose profit over the neurological health of billions.
why_it_matters: Leaded gasoline went on to contaminate the entire planet for seventy years, causing measurable drops in IQ across multiple generations and contributing to elevated rates of violence and developmental disorders worldwide. Researchers now estimate that over 800 million children globally suffered irreversible lead exposure before the additive was finally banned in most countries. The Bayway disaster and Hamilton's ignored testimony established the template — still operative today with tobacco, PFAS, and climate disinformation — by which industries manufacture doubt to delay regulation of known poisons.
